claims.claim: The identity of NC products correlates with their position along the anteroposterior (A-P) axis, which is in turn reflected by the expression of HOX gene paralogous groups (PGs).
claims.source: The identity of NC products correlates with their position along the anteroposterior (A-P) axis, which is in turn reflected by the expression of HOX gene paralogous groups (PGs).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neural crest cell identity.

claims.claim: Cranial NC cells give rise to mesoectodermal derivatives (e.g. dermis, cartilage, bone), melanocytes, neurons and glia colonizing the head.
claims.source: Cranial NC cells give rise to mesoectodermal derivatives (e.g. dermis, cartilage, bone), melanocytes, neurons and glia colonizing the head (Le Douarin et al., 2004)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cranial NC cells are divided into an anterior HOX-negative and a posterior HOX PG (1-3)-positive domain.
claims.source: Cranial NC cells give rise to mesoectodermal derivatives (e.g. dermis, cartilage, bone), melanocytes, neurons and glia colonizing the head (Le Douarin et al., 2004) and are divided into an anterior HOX-negative and a posterior HOX PG (1-3 )-positive domain.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cardiac NC cells contribute to heart structures.
claims.source: The latter also includes cells contributing to heart structures (termed cardiac NC) (Le Douarin et al., 2004; Kirby et al., 1983).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Vagal NC cells are located between somites 1–7 and are marked by the expression of HOX PG(3-5) members.
claims.source: Vagal NC cells, which are located between somites 1–7, are marked by the expression of HOX PG(3-5) members (Kam and Lui, 2015; Fu et al., 2003; Chan et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Vagal NC cells generate the enteric nervous system (ENS).
claims.source: Vagal NC cells, which are located between somites 1–7, are marked by the expression of HOX PG(3-5) members (Kam and Lui, 2015; Fu et al., 2003; Chan et al., 2005) and generate the enteric nervous system (ENS) (Le Douarin and Teillet, 1973).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: HOX PG(5-9)-positive NC cells at the trunk level produce sympathoadrenal cells, which in turn give rise to sympathetic neurons, neuroendocrine cells, and melanocytes.
claims.source: HOX PG(5-9) -positive NC cells at the trunk level (Kam and Lui, 2015; Nguyen et al., 2009; Ishikawa and Ito, 2009; Huber et al., 2012) produce sympathoadrenal cells, which in turn give rise to sympathetic neurons, neuroendocrine cells, and melanocytes (Le Douarin and Teillet, 1974).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Conventional protocols to obtain NC from hPSCs are based on the production of a neurectodermal intermediate via TGFβ signalling inhibition, which is subsequently steered toward a NC fate through stimulation of WNT activity combined with appropriate levels of BMP signalling.
claims.source: Conventional protocols to obtain NC from hPSCs are based on the production of a neurectodermal intermediate, via TGFβ signalling inhibition, which is subsequently steered toward a NC fate, usually through stimulation of WNT activity combined with the appropriate levels of BMP signalling (Lee et al., 2007; Menendez et al., 2011; Chambers et al., 2012; Hackland et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Conventional NC differentiation strategies yield NC cells of an anterior cranial character lacking HOX gene expression.
claims.source: These strategies yield NC cells of an anterior cranial character lacking HOX gene expression
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The generation of more posterior HOX+ NC subtypes typically relies on the addition of retinoic acid (RA) and/or further WNT signalling stimulation.
claims.source: the generation of more posterior HOX+ NC subtypes typically relies on the addition of retinoic acid (RA) and/or further WNT signalling stimulation (Huang et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2016; Denham et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: RA and WNT signalling fail to efficiently induce a high number of NC cells of a HOX PG(5-9)+ trunk identity from an anterior cranial progenitor.
claims.source: However, these signals fail to efficiently induce a high number of NC cells of a HOX PG(5-9) +trunk identity from an anterior cranial progenitor.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current protocols based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claims.claim: The generation of trunk NC derivatives such as sympathoadrenal cells often requires the flow cytometry-based purification of small cell populations positive for lineage-specific fluorescent reporter or cell surface markers.
claims.source: Therefore, the generation of trunk NC derivatives such as sympathoadrenal cells often requires the flow cytometry-based purification of small cell populations positive for lineage-specific fluorescent reporter (Oh et al., 2016) or cell surface markers (Abu-Bonsrah et al., 2018), a time-consuming and laborious approach.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Studies in chicken and mouse embryos employing fate mapping and lineage tracing have shown the existence of a posterior NC progenitor entity, which is distinct from its more anterior counterparts and potentially co-localises with a pool of caudally-located axial progenitors.
claims.source: A number of studies in chicken and mouse embryos employing both fate mapping and lineage tracing have shown the existence of a posterior NC progenitor entity, which is distinct from its more anterior counterparts and potentially co-localises with a pool of caudally-located axial progenitors (Catala et al., 1995; Albors et al., 2016; Javali et al., 2017; Schoenwolf et al., 1985; Schoenwolf and Nichols, 1984; Wymeersch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Axial progenitors include a bipotent stem cell-like population that fuels embryonic axis elongation through the coordinated production of spinal cord neurectoderm and paraxial mesoderm (PXM).
claims.source: These progenitors include a bipotent stem cell-like population that fuels embryonic axis elongation through the coordinated production of spinal cord neurectoderm and paraxial mesoderm (PXM) (Tzouanacou et al., 2009)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In both mouse and chick embryos neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) are located in the node/streak border and the caudal lateral epiblast during early somitogenesis, and later in the chordoneural hinge within the tailbud (TB).
claims.source: In both mouse and chick embryos these neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) are located in the node/streak border and the caudal lateral epiblast during early somitogenesis, and later in the chordoneural hinge within the tailbud (TB) (Wymeersch et al., 2016; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Cambray and Wilson, 2002; Brown and Storey, 2000; McGrew et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: No unique NMP markers have been determined to date.
claims.source: No unique NMP markers have been determined to date
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: NMPs are molecularly defined by the co-expression of the pro-mesodermal transcription factor Brachyury (T) and neural regulator SOX2.
claims.source: molecularly, NMPs are defined by the co-expression of the pro-mesodermal transcription factor Brachyury (T) and neural regulator SOX2 (Tsakiridis et al., 2014; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; ).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: NMPs express transcripts which are also present in the primitive streak (PS) and TB, marking committed PXM and posterior neurectodermal progenitors such as Cdx and Hox gene family members, Tbx6 and Nkx1-2.
claims.source: Furthermore, they express transcripts which are also present in the primitive streak (PS) and TB, marking committed PXM and posterior neurectodermal progenitors such as Cdx and Hox gene family members, Tbx6 and Nkx1-2 (Albors et al., 2016; Javali et al., 2017; Cambray and Wilson, 2007; Gouti et al., 2017; Amin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: T and SOX2 have a critical role, in conjunction with CDX and HOX proteins, in regulating the balance between NMP maintenance and differentiation by integrating inputs predominantly from the WNT and FGF signalling pathways.
claims.source: T and SOX2 have a critical role, in conjunction with CDX and HOX proteins, in regulating the balance between NMP maintenance and differentiation by integrating inputs predominantly from the WNT and FGF signalling pathways (Wymeersch et al., 2016; Gouti et al., 2017; Amin et al., 2016; Young et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Combined stimulation of WNT and FGF signalling pathways results in the robust induction of T+SOX2+ NMP like cells from mouse and human PSCs.
claims.source: The pivotal role of these pathways has been further demonstrated by recent studies showing that their combined stimulation results in the robust induction of T + SOX2+ NMP like cells from mouse and human PSCs (Turner et al., 2014; Lippmann et al., 2015; Gouti et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: NMPs/axial progenitors appear to be closely related to trunk NC precursors in vivo.
claims.source: NMPs/axial progenitors appear to be closely related to trunk NC precursors in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the literature cited in the following sentences.

claims.claim: Trunk NC production has been shown to be controlled by transcription factors which also regulate cell fate decisions in axial progenitors such as CDX proteins and NKX1-2.
claims.source: Specifically, trunk NC production has been shown to be controlled by transcription factors which also regulate cell fate decisions in axial progenitors such as CDX proteins (Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2012; Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2014; Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2016) and NKX1-2 (Sasai et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Fate mapping experiments involving the grafting of a portion of E8.5 mouse caudal lateral epiblast T+SOX2+ cells have revealed the presence of localised cell populations exhibiting simultaneously mesodermal, neural and NC differentiation potential.
claims.source: The close relationship between bipotent axial and posterior NC progenitors is further supported by fate mapping experiments involving the grafting of a portion of E8.5 mouse caudal lateral epiblast T+SOX2+ cells (Wymeersch et al., 2016) and avian embryonic TB regions (Catala et al., 1995; McGrew et al., 2008) which have revealed the presence of localised cell populations exhibiting simultaneously mesodermal, neural and NC differentiation potential.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Retrospective clonal analysis in mouse embryos has shown that some posterior NC cells originate from progenitors which also generate PXM and spinal cord neurectoderm.
claims.source: Furthermore, retrospective clonal analysis in mouse embryos has shown that some posterior NC cells originate from progenitors which also generate PXM and spinal cord neurectoderm (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Lineage tracing experiments employing NMP markers such as T, Nkx1-2, Foxb1 and Tbx6 as Cre drivers show that axial progenitor descendants include NC cells at caudal levels.
claims.source: This finding is in line with lineage tracing experiments employing NMP markers such as T (Anderson et al., 2013; Feller et al., 2008; Garriock et al., 2015; Perantoni et al., 2005), Nkx1-2 (Albors et al., 2016), Foxb1 (Turner et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2007) and Tbx6 (Javali et al., 2017) as Cre drivers showing that axial progenitor descendants include NC cells at caudal levels.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The trunk/lumbar NC is likely to originate from a subset of axial progenitors arising near the PS/TB.
claims.source: Together these findings suggest that the trunk/lumbar NC is likely to originate from a subset of axial progenitors arising near the PS/TB.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claims.claim: Combined stimulation of the WNT and FGF signalling pathways in PSCs leads to the production of a high (>80%) percentage of T+SOX2+ cells.
claims.source: We and others have previously shown that combined stimulation of the WNT and FGF signalling pathways in PSCs leads to the production of a high (>80%) percentage of T+SOX2+ cells.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: T+SOX2+ cells resulting from WNT-FGF treatment resemble embryonic posterior axial progenitors, including NMPs, both in terms of marker expression and developmental potential.
claims.source: The resulting cultures resemble embryonic posterior axial progenitors, including NMPs, both in terms of marker expression and developmental potential (Gouti et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2014; Lippmann et al., 2015; Gouti et al., 2014; Tsakiridis and Wilson, 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Most cells emerging under WNT-FGF treatment conditions co-expressed T and SOX2 as well as CDX2.
claims.source: As reported previously, most cells emerging under these conditions co-expressed T and SOX2 as well as CDX2 (Figure 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The transcriptomes of axial progenitors/NMPs and hPSCs were distinct from each other.
claims.source: We found that the transcriptomes of axial progenitors/NMPs and hPSCs were distinct from each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: 1911 and 1895 genes were significantly (padj <0.05; Fold Change ≥ 2) up- and down-regulated in axial progenitors compared to hPSCs respectively.
claims.source: marked global gene expression changes accompanying the acquisition of an axial progenitor character: 1911 and 1895 genes were significantly (padj <0.05; Fold Change ≥ 2) up- and down-regulated compared to hPSCs respectively (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claims.claim: The most-downregulated genes in axial progenitors were associated with undifferentiated hPSCs (e.g. NANOG, GDF3, POU5F1), anterior neurectoderm (OTX2) and lateral/ventral mesoderm (KDR).
claims.source: Predictably, the most-downregulated genes were associated with undifferentiated hPSCs (e.g. NANOG, GDF3, POU5F1), anterior neurectoderm (OTX2) and lateral/ventral mesoderm (KDR).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claims.claim: The vast majority of the top-upregulated genes in axial progenitors were well-established drivers of axis elongation (e.g. TBRA, CDX1/2, EVX1, MSGN1, TBX6) and WNT/FGF/NOTCH/RA signalling pathway components.
claims.source: The vast majority of the top-upregulated genes were well-established drivers of axis elongation (e.g. TBRA, CDX1/2, EVX1, MSGN1, TBX6) and WNT/FGF/NOTCH/RA signalling pathway components, known to be expressed at high levels in the late PS/TB regions in vivo (e.g. WNT3A/5B, RSPO3, FGF4/8, FGF17, HES7) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis and shown in figures.

claims.claim: A large fraction of upregulated genes in axial progenitors were transcriptional regulators.
claims.source: A large fraction of upregulated genes were transcriptional regulators (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis and shown in figures.

claims.claim: Members of HOX PGs 1-9 were strongly differentially expressed between axial progenitors and hPSCs.
claims.source: we found that members of HOX PGs 1-9 were strongly differentially expressed between the two groups (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis and shown in figures.

claims.claim: The upregulation of posterior thoracic PG(5-9) HOX transcripts and the presence of many transcripts marking 'late' E9.5 mouse embryonic NMPs suggest that day 3 WNT-FGF-treated hPSC cultures may correspond to a more developmentally advanced axial progenitor state.
claims.source: The upregulation of posterior thoracic PG(5-9) HOX transcripts as well as the presence of many transcripts (23/32) marking 'late' E9.5 mouse embryonic NMPs such as CYP26A1, FGF17 and WNT5A (Gouti et al., 2017) suggest that day 3 WNT-FGF-treated hPSC cultures may correspond to a more developmentally advanced axial progenitor state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with published mouse NMP data.

claims.claim: A considerable number of genes known to mark the neural plate border and early NC in vivo were significantly upregulated in axial progenitors.
claims.source: The RNAseq analysis revealed that a considerable number of genes known to mark the neural plate border and early NC in vivo ('NC/border' e.g. SOX9, PAX3, MSX1/2, SNAI1/2, ZIC1/3) were also significantly upregulated in axial progenitors (Figure 2A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis and shown in figures.

claims.claim: The upregulation of NC/border markers in axial progenitors was verified using quantitative real time PCR (qPCR).
claims.source: a finding which was verified using quantitative real time PCR (qPCR) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A considerable fraction (~40–60% in two different hPSC lines) of T+ cells also expressed the early NC markers/specifiers SOX9, SNAI2 and PAX3.
claims.source: Immunostaining of d3 WNT-FGF-treated hPSC cultures showed that a considerable fraction (~40–60% in two different hPSC lines) of T+ cells also expressed the early NC markers/specifiers SOX9, SNAI2 and PAX3 (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SOX9-positive cells were found to express low or no MSGN1 or TBX6.
claims.source: Moreover, SOX9-positive cells were found to express low or no MSGN1 or TBX6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The upregulation of NC/border markers following WNT-FGF treatment of hPSCs was unlikely to reflect the presence of committed PXM cells.
claims.source: suggesting that the upregulation of NC/border markers following WNT-FGF treatment of hPSCs was unlikely to reflect the presence of committed PXM cells given that some of these genes are also expressed in the mesoderm during axis elongation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SOX9+ cells do not express mesodermal markers.

claims.claim: A NC/border state arises within multipotent posterior axial progenitors which have not committed to a neural or mesodermal fate.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings indicate that a NC/border state arises within multipotent posterior axial progenitors which have not committed to a neural or mesodermal fate.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing co-expression of T and NC markers without mesodermal commitment markers.

claims.claim: Many BMP pathway-associated transcripts (BMP2/4/6/7 and ID1/4) were significantly upregulated in axial progenitors compared to hPSCs.
claims.source: RNAseq revealed that many BMP pathway -associated transcripts (BMP2/4/6/7 and ID1/4) were significantly upregulated compared to hPSCs (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis and shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Axial progenitor cultures exhibit expression of phosphorylated SMAD1/5, a readout of BMP activity.
claims.source: Moreover, antibody staining showed expression of phosphorylated SMAD1/5, a readout of BMP activity (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: BMP activity is extinguished upon treatment with the BMP antagonist LDN193189 (LDN) during the in vitro differentiation of hPSCs to day three axial progenitors.
claims.source: This is extinguished upon treatment with the BMP antagonist LDN193189 (LDN) (Cuny et al., 2008) during the in vitro differentiation of hPSCs to day three axial progenitors (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: BMP inhibition caused a decrease in the transcript levels of some NC/border-specific transcripts such as PAX3, SNAI1 and MSX1.
claims.source: Interestingly, BMP inhibition caused a decrease in the transcript levels of some NC/border-specific transcripts such as PAX3, SNAI1 and MSX1 (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: BMP inhibition caused a reduction in the expression of the NMP/late PS/TB markers CDX2, WNT3A and T, although only the downregulation in the levels of T was statistically significant.
claims.source: We also observed a reduction in the expression of the NMP/late PS/TB markers CDX2, WNT3A and T (Figure 2E) although only the downregulation in the levels of the latter was statistically significant.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: BMP signalling contributes to maintenance of T expression in the mouse tailbud.
claims.source: This is consistent with a recent report showing that BMP signalling contributes to maintenance of T expression in the mouse tailbud (Sharma et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The PXM specifier TBX6 remained relatively unaffected by LDN treatment.
claims.source: We also found that the PXM specifier TBX6 remained relatively unaffected by LDN treatment suggesting that emergence of prospective PXM is not influenced by BMP inhibition (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: SOX2 expression was significantly increased upon LDN treatment.
claims.source: By contrast, SOX2 expression was significantly increased upon LDN treatment (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Endogenous BMP activity is associated with the acquisition of a SOX2+low border/NC identity by posterior axial progenitors while transition toward a SOX2+high neural fate relies on BMP antagonism in vitro.
claims.source: Taken together these data indicate an association between endogenous BMP activity and the acquisition of a SOX2+ low border/NC identity by posterior axial progenitors while transition toward a SOX2+ high neural fate relies on BMP antagonism in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BMP inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: Culture of day 3 WNT-FGF-treated hPSCs under NC-inducing conditions for 5–6 days gave rise to a high number (average percentage = 50% of total cells) of cells co-expressing the definitive NC marker SOX10 together with HOXC9, a readout of trunk axial identity.
claims.source: Culture of day 3 WNT-FGF-treated hPSCs under these NC-inducing conditions for 5–6 days gave rise to a high number (average percentage = 50% of total cells) of cells co-expressing the definitive NC marker SOX10 together with HOXC9, a readout of trunk axial identity (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in the figures.

claims.claim: No nuclear staining above background intensity levels with the monoclonal HOXC9 antibody was observed in negative control undifferentiated hPSCs or ETS1+ NC cells generated using the cranial NC induction protocol.
claims.source: We observed no nuclear staining above background intensity levels with the monoclonal HOXC9 antibody we employed in negative control undifferentiated hPSCs or ETS1+ NC cells generated using our cranial NC induction protocol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) (Simoes-Costa and Bronner, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: A large proportion of the trunk NC cultures were SOX9+HOXC9+.
claims.source: A large proportion of the cultures were also SOX9+ HOXC9+ further confirming a trunk NC character
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: The percentage of neural cells marked by SOX1 expression remained very low throughout the course of the differentiation toward trunk NC.
claims.source: whereas the percentage of neural cells marked by SOX1 expression remained very low throughout the course of the differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Posterior NC progenitors do not progress through neural commitment but rather diverge from an earlier pre-neural, border-like stage.
claims.source: This may indicate that posterior NC progenitors do not progress through neural commitment but rather diverge from an earlier pre-neural, border-like stage reflecting previous reports which show that NC specification takes place prior to definitive neurulation (Sasai et al., 2014; Leung et al., 2016; Basch et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the low SOX1 expression and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: During the transition toward trunk neural crest, the NMP/pre-neural marker NKX1-2 was rapidly extinguished followed shortly after by T, while CDX1 transcript levels declined more slowly.
claims.source: Furthermore, during the transition toward trunk neural crest, the NMP/pre-neural marker NKX1-2 was rapidly extinguished followed shortly after by T, while CDX1 transcript levels declined more slowly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The expression of CDX2 and SOX9 was maintained at high levels throughout the course of differentiation of axial progenitors to trunk NC.
claims.source: By contrast, the expression of CDX2 and SOX9 was maintained at high levels throughout the course of differentiation of axial progenitors to trunk NC
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: SOX10 expression appeared only after day 7 of differentiation.
claims.source: while SOX10 expression appeared only after day 7 of differentiation (Day 0 defined as the start of axial progenitor induction from hPSCs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F, data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Grafted human axial progenitor-derived trunk NC cells migrated out of the graft site in chick embryos (6/6 grafted embryos).
claims.source: We found that, following incubation for 2–3 days, grafted donor cells migrated out of the graft site (6/6 grafted embryos) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from chick embryo grafting experiments shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Grafted human axial progenitor-derived trunk NC cells that had migrated the furthest consistently entered the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and exhibited expression of DRG markers such as TUBB3, ISL1 and SOX10 (3/6 grafted embryos).
claims.source: Furthermore, the donor cells that had migrated the furthest consistently entered the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and exhibited expression of DRG markers such as TUBB3 (Shao et al., 2017) (Figure 3D), ISL1 (Ericson et al., 1992) and SOX10 (Ota et al., 2004) (3/6 grafted embryos) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from chick embryo grafting experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Human trunk NC generated from axial progenitors exhibits similar migratory behaviour/in vivo differentiation potential to its embryonic counterparts.
claims.source: These results suggest that human trunk NC generated from axial progenitors exhibits similar migratory behaviour/in vivo differentiation potential to its embryonic counterparts.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chick embryo grafting experiments.

claims.claim: LDN treatment of axial progenitors during their induction from hPSCs (i.e. between days 0–3 of differentiation) has no effect on subsequent trunk NC production.
claims.source: We found that LDN treatment of axial progenitors during their induction from hPSCs (i.e. between days 0–3 of differentiation) has no effect on subsequent trunk NC production (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Early BMP activity alone is not the critical determinant of NC potency in axial progenitor populations.
claims.source: indicating that early BMP activity alone is not the critical determinant of NC potency in this population.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the LDN treatment experiment.

claims.claim: Treatment of axial progenitors with high levels of FGF2-CHIR led to the production of TBX6+/MSGN1+ PXM.
claims.source: We also confirmed the NM potency of the starting axial progenitor cultures as treatment with high levels of FGF2-CHIR and RA led to the production of TBX6+/MSGN1 + PXM and SOX1+ spinal cord, posterior neurectoderm (PNE) cells respectively (Figure 3A and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and qPCR data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Treatment of axial progenitors with RA led to the production of SOX1+ spinal cord, posterior neurectoderm (PNE) cells.
claims.source: We also confirmed the NM potency of the starting axial progenitor cultures as treatment with high levels of FGF2-CHIR and RA led to the production of TBX6+/MSGN1 + PXM and SOX1+ spinal cord, posterior neurectoderm (PNE) cells respectively (Figure 3A and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: hPSC-derived NM-potent axial progenitor cultures are competent to produce trunk NC at high efficiency.
claims.source: Taken together these data suggest that hPSC-derived NM-potent axial progenitor cultures are competent to produce trunk NC at high efficiency.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing trunk NC generation from axial progenitors.

claims.claim: T-VENUS+ axial progenitors exhibited no or very low (5% of total cells) expression of the definitive pluripotency markers OTX2 and NANOG respectively.
claims.source: T-VENUS+ axial progenitors exhibited no or very low (5% of total cells) expression of the definitive pluripotency markers OTX2 and NANOG (Acampora et al., 2013; Osorno et al., 2012) respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: T-VENUS+ axial progenitors are unlikely to be pluripotent.
claims.source: T-VENUS+ axial progenitors exhibited no or very low (5% of total cells) expression of the definitive pluripotency markers OTX2 and NANOG (Acampora et al., 2013; Osorno et al., 2012) respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and hence are unlikely to be pluripotent.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of pluripotency marker expression.

claims.claim: The small NANOG+T-VENUS+low fraction detected probably reflects the reported presence of Nanog transcripts in the gastrulation-stage posterior epiblast of mouse embryos.
claims.source: The small NANOG + T-VENUS+low fraction we detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C) probably reflects the reported presence of Nanog transcripts in the gastrulation-stage posterior epiblast of mouse embryos (Teo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with published mouse data.

claims.claim: Almost 60% of sorted T-VENUS+high cells were SOX10+ after 5 days in NC-inducing conditions, and about a third of them also co-expressed HOXC9.
claims.source: We found that almost 60% of the cells were SOX10+ and about a third of them also co-expressed HOXC9 (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in the figure.

claims.claim: T+ hPSC derived axial progenitors have the ability to generate efficiently SOX10+ neural crest.
claims.source: This finding demonstrates that T + hPSC derived axial progenitors have the ability to generate efficiently SOX10+ neural crest
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the T-VENUS sorting experiment.

claims.claim: At least half of the trunk NC cells derived from bulk axial progenitor cultures originate from T-expressing cells.
claims.source: and suggests that at least half of the trunk NC cells derived from bulk axial progenitor cultures (Figure 3B,C) originate from T-expressing cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the T-VENUS sorting experiment results.

claims.claim: Most current NC differentiation protocols aiming to generate posterior (e.g. trunk) cell populations from hPSCs rely on the caudalisation of an anterior ectodermal precursor via treatment with RA and/or WNT agonists.
claims.source: Similar to established in vitro neural induction strategies, most current NC differentiation protocols aiming to generate posterior (e.g. trunk) cell populations from hPSCs rely on the caudalisation of an anterior ectodermal precursor via treatment with RA and/or WNT agonists (Chambers et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2016; Denham et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: RA-treated NC cells expressed high levels of HOX PG(1-5) members compared to untreated NC suggesting a posterior cranial and vagal/cardiac NC character.
claims.source: In line with previous findings (Huang et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2016) RA-treated cells expressed high levels of HOX PG(1-5) members compared to untreated NC suggesting a posterior cranial and vagal/cardiac NC character (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Efficient induction of trunk HOXC8 and 9 transcripts was only achieved when posterior axial progenitors were employed as the starting population for NC generation.
claims.source: However, efficient induction of trunk HOXC8 and 9 transcripts was only achieved when posterior axial progenitors were employed as the starting population for NC generation (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Axial progenitor-derived NC cells were marked by increased expression of the trunk NC marker HES6, but did not express the cranial markers OTX2, DMBX1 and LHX5.
claims.source: Furthermore, axial progenitor-derived NC cells were marked by increased expression of the trunk NC marker HES6, but did not express the cranial markers OTX2, DMBX1 and LHX5 although they were positive for the 'late' cranial NC transcripts (TFA2B, ETS1, SOX8) (Simoes-Costa and Bronner, 2016) (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Posterior axial progenitors are the ideal starting population for efficiently generating trunk NC in vitro.
claims.source: We thus conclude that posterior axial progenitors are the ideal starting population for efficiently generating trunk NC in vitro
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different NC induction strategies.

claims.claim: RA treatment of anterior NC precursors predominantly produces posterior cranial and cardiac/vagal NC cells.
claims.source: whereas RA treatment of anterior NC precursors predominantly produces posterior cranial and cardiac/vagal NC cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different NC induction strategies.

claims.claim: Trunk NC precursors are likely to arise within cells with axial progenitor/NMP features rather than a caudalised anterior progenitor.
claims.source: These data also serve as evidence supporting the notion that trunk NC precursors are likely to arise within cells with axial progenitor/NMP features rather than a caudalised anterior progenitor.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different NC induction strategies.

claims.claim: T-VENUS+highOTX2 negative axial progenitors are a source of trunk NC.
claims.source: This is further supported by our T-VENUS sorting experiments showing that T-VENUS+highOTX2 negative axial progenitors are a source of trunk NC (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from the T-VENUS sorting experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The generation of trunk NC cells is unlikely to occur via 'caudalisation' of an anterior OTX2+ NC precursor.
claims.source: and therefore the generation of these cells is unlikely to occur via 'caudalisation' of an anterior OTX2+ NC precursor.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the T-VENUS sorting experiments.

claims.claim: Axial progenitor-derived NC cells (NMP-NC d9) and their precursors (NMP-NC d6) grouped together and were distinct from a cluster containing d6 anterior cranial NC (ANC) and +RA NC cells and their common d3 progenitor (ANC d3).
claims.source: We found that axial progenitor-derived NC cells (NMP-NC d9) and their precursors (NMP-NC d6) grouped together and were distinct from a cluster containing d6 anterior cranial NC (ANC) and +RA NC cells and their common d3 progenitor (ANC d3) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The three final NC populations (ANC, +RA, NMP-NC) exhibited distinct transcriptional profiles.
claims.source: Although the three final populations exhibited distinct transcriptional profiles (Figure 4C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: All three NC populations (ANC, +RA, NMP-NC) expressed pan-NC genes including 'early' NC/border (MSX1/2, PAX3/7)- and 'late' NC (SOX10, SNAI1/2)-associated transcription factors.
claims.source: they all expressed pan-NC genes including 'early' NC/border (MSX1/2, PAX3/7)- and 'late' NC (SOX10, SNAI1/2)-associated transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: ANC cells failed to express any HOX transcripts.
claims.source: In line with our previous observations (Figure 3G), ANC cells failed to express any HOX transcripts
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: RA treatment induced anterior HOX genes.
claims.source: RA treatment induced anterior HOX genes
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: Only WNT-FGF-treated hPSCs gave rise to NC cells positive for thoracic HOX PG(5-9) members.
claims.source: and only WNT-FGF-treated hPSCs gave rise to NC cells positive for thoracic HOX PG(5-9) members (Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The simultaneous presence of anterior HOX PG(1-5) transcripts together with their more posterior group 6–9 counterparts in trunk NC cultures would be expected in trunk NC due to their co-expression in the posterior neural tube/neural crest in E9.5 mouse embryos.
claims.source: The simultaneous presence of anterior HOX PG(1-5) transcripts together with their more posterior group 6–9 counterparts in our trunk NC cultures would be expected in trunk NC due to their co-expression in the posterior neural tube/neural crest in E9.5 mouse embryos (Gouti et al., 2017; Arenkiel et al., 2003; Bel et al., 1998; Glaser et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with published mouse data.

claims.claim: The simultaneous presence of anterior HOX PG(1-5) transcripts together with their more posterior group 6–9 counterparts in trunk NC cultures might result from the co-emergence of a separate population of cardiac/vagal NC cells during trunk NC differentiation due to the action of endogenous RA signalling.
claims.source: It might also result from the co-emergence of a separate population of cardiac/vagal NC cells during trunk NC differentiation due to the action of endogenous RA signalling since our microarray data revealed the upregulation of RA signalling components in axial progenitor-derived trunk NC (Supplementary file 2) even though no exogenous RA was added to the differentiation medium.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the microarray data.

claims.claim: Some of the most-upregulated transcripts in +RA cells were established posterior cranial (e.g. ALX1/3), cardiac (e.g. FOXC1 and 2; PDGFRa; TBX2/3) and vagal/enteric NC markers (PHOX2A; KITLG; ARPC1B).
claims.source: The axial identity of the resulting posterior NC subtypes was further confirmed by the observation that some of the most-upregulated transcripts in +RA cells were established posterior cranial (e.g. ALX1/3 [Lumb et al., 2017]), cardiac (e.g. FOXC1 and 2 (Seo and Kume, 2006); PDGFRa (Tallquist and Soriano, 2003); TBX2/3 [Mesbah et al., 2012]) and vagal/enteric NC markers (PHOX2A (Young et al., 1999); KITLG (Torihashi et al., 1996); ARPC1B (Iwashita et al., 2003) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Known trunk NC, sympathoadrenal and sympathetic/sensory neuron regulators such as CDX2, INSM1, NEUROG1 and ISL1 were induced only in NC cells derived from axial progenitors.
claims.source: In contrast, known trunk NC, sympathoadrenal and sympathetic/sensory neuron regulators such as CDX2 (Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2016), INSM1 (Wildner et al., 2008), NEUROG1 (Perez et al., 1999) (Figure 4F) and ISL1 (Huber et al., 2013) (Supplementary file 2) were induced only in NC cells derived from axial progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: ASLX3, the human homologue of the Drosophila polycomb protein asx, is a novel trunk NC marker.
claims.source: We also identified ASLX3, the human homologue of the Drosophila polycomb protein asx (Katoh and Katoh, 2004) which has been recently linked to the developmental syndrome Bainbridge-Ropers (Bainbridge et al., 2013) as a novel trunk NC marker (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a novel finding from the microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: Transcription factors specifically induced in anterior cranial NC cells included the forkhead gene FOXS1 and TCF7L2.
claims.source: Transcription factors specifically induced in anterior cranial NC cells included the forkhead gene FOXS1 which has been shown to be expressed in mouse NC derivatives (Heglind et al., 2005) and TCF7L2, a WNT signalling effector which has been reported to harbour a NC-associated enhancer (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2012) (Supplementary file 2, 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A mixed posterior cranial/vagal/cardiac NC character arises upon treatment of anterior NC precursors with RA whereas a bona fide trunk NC identity can be achieved only via an axial progenitor intermediate.
claims.source: Collectively these data support the idea that a mixed posterior cranial/vagal/cardiac NC character arises upon treatment of anterior NC precursors with RA whereas a bona fide trunk NC identity can be achieved only via an axial progenitor intermediate.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: One of the most over-represented gene categories in all three axial NC subtypes were transcription factors.
claims.source: One of the most over-represented gene categories in all three axial NC subtypes were transcription factors
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: A common NC-specific transcription factor module was found to be expressed regardless of axial character.
claims.source: and a common NC-specific transcription factor module was found to be expressed regardless of axial character (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 3, 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The common NC-specific transcription factor module included well-established NC/border regulators such as PAX3/7, MSX2, SOX9/10, TFAP2A-C and SNAI1/2.
claims.source: This included well-established NC/border regulators such as PAX3/7, MSX2, SOX9/10, TFAP2A-C and SNAI1/2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 3, 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The expression levels of many NC transcription factors varied between the three NC groups.
claims.source: However, the expression levels of many of these transcription factors varied between the three groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The highest levels of HES6 and MSX1 were found in axial progenitor-derived trunk NC cells and their precursors.
claims.source: The highest levels of HES6 and MSX1 were found in axial progenitor-derived trunk NC cells and their precursors
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: High PAX7 and SNAI1/SOX9 expression was more prevalent in the anterior cranial and RA-treated samples respectively.
claims.source: whereas high PAX7 and SNAI1/SOX9 expression was more prevalent in the anterior cranial and RA-treated samples respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Expression of LHX5 and DMBX1 marks an anterior NC state whereas HES6 is associated exclusively with a trunk fate.
claims.source: Comparison of the day six trunk and d3 ANC precursor transcriptomes also revealed that expression of LHX5 and DMBX1 marks an anterior NC state whereas HES6 is associated exclusively with a trunk fate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Diversification of axial identity in NC cells starts at an early time point via the action of distinct molecular players.
claims.source: indicating that diversification of axial identity in NC cells starts at an early time point via the action of distinct molecular players.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: Dramatic global gene expression changes take place during the axial progenitor-trunk NC transition.
claims.source: We found that dramatic global gene expression changes take place during the axial progenitor-trunk NC transition (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Some of the most upregulated transcripts during the axial progenitor-trunk NC transition were the NC-specific TFAP2A/B, ETS1, SOX5 and SOX10 together with the established trunk NC specifier CDX2, the novel trunk NC marker ASLX3, the nuclear receptors NR2F1/2 and thoracic HOX genes (HOXB7, B9).
claims.source: Some of the most upregulated transcripts were the NC-specific TFAP2A/B, ETS1, SOX5 and SOX10 together with the established trunk NC specifier CDX2, the novel trunk NC marker ASLX3, the nuclear receptors NR2F1/2 and thoracic HOX genes (HOXB7, B9) (Figure 4G, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Signature axial progenitor transcription factors (MIXL1, T, NKX1-2), anterior HOX genes (HOXA1/B1) and some WNT signalling components (WNT8A/5B) were significantly downregulated during the axial progenitor-trunk NC transition.
claims.source: In contrast, signature axial progenitor transcription factors (MIXL1, T, NKX1-2) (Figure 4G, Supplementary file 4), anterior HOX genes (HOXA1/B1) and some WNT signalling components (WNT8A/5B) were significantly downregulated (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Differentiation of trunk NC precursors appears to involve the transition from an axial progenitor-associated gene regulatory network to a NC-specifying one that incorporates factors which potentially act as general determinants of posterior cell fate (CDX2, HOXB9).
claims.source: Thus, differentiation of trunk NC precursors appears to involve the transition from an axial progenitor-associated gene regulatory network to a NC-specifying one that incorporates factors which potentially act as general determinants of posterior cell fate (CDX2, HOXB9).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: The most-highly induced transcripts in posterior cranial/cardiac/vagal NC cells included the RA receptors beta and gamma (RARb/g) and the T-box transcription factor TBX2.
claims.source: The most-highly induced transcripts in posterior cranial/cardiac/vagal NC cells included the RA receptors beta and gamma (RARb/g) which have been involved in hindbrain and neural crest patterning (Dupé et al., 1999) and the T-box transcription factor TBX2, a marker of cardiac NC and in vitro derived vagal/enteric NC progenitors (Fattahi et al., 2016) (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Other upregulated transcripts in posterior cranial/cardiac/vagal NC cells included the planar cell polarity (PCP) component PRICKLE1 and the TGFβ signalling-associated gene TGFBI.
claims.source: Other upregulated transcripts included the planar cell polarity (PCP) component PRICKLE1, a regulator of cardiac NC cell function (Gibbs et al., 2016) and the TGFβ signalling-associated gene TGFBI (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Anterior NC d3 precursor specific transcripts included the border markers PAX7 and ZIC3 as well as the early cranial NC transcription factors OTX2 and LHX5.
claims.source: Anterior NC d3 precursor specific –transcripts included the border markers PAX7 and ZIC3 as well as the early cranial NC transcription factors OTX2 and LHX5 ( Simoes-Costa and Bronner, 2016) (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Posterior cranial/cardiac/vagal NC cells arise from an anterior neural plate border precursor through posteriorisation under the influence of RA and possibly the non-canonical WNT and TGFβ pathways.
claims.source: These results indicate that, in contrast to trunk NC cells, posterior crania/cardiac/vagal NC cells arise from an anterior neural plate border precursor through posteriorisation under the influence of RA and possibly the non-canonical WNT and TGFβ pathways.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray data analysis.

claims.claim: The BMP and sonic hedgehog (SHH) signalling pathways have been shown to be critical for the specification of sympathoadrenal lineages from NC cells.
claims.source: The BMP and sonic hedgehog (SHH) signalling pathways have been shown to be critical for the specification of these lineages from NC cells (Oh et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 1999; Morikawa et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The majority of trunk NC cells cultured in BMP4 and SHH agonists for 4 days were PHOX2B expressing (average percentage from four independent experiments = 73.5%, s.d. = 6.3).
claims.source: FACS analysis revealed that the majority of cells were PHOX2B expressing (average percentage from four independent experiments = 73.5%, s.d. = 6.3) (Figure 5B)
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A large proportion of PHOX2B+ cells were also positive for the early SA progenitor marker ASCL1 indicating that they had acquired a symphathoadrenal identity.
claims.source: and a large proportion of them were also positive for the early SA progenitor marker ASCL1 (Hirsch et al., 1998) indicating that they had acquired a symphathoadrenal identity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Further maturation of SA progenitors in the presence of neurotrophic factors (BDNF, GDNF and NGF) resulted in the induction of a high yield of sympathetic neurons/progenitors co-expressing PHOX2B together with GATA3 (average of 40% of total cells), ASCL1 (63%) and ISL1 (64%).
claims.source: Further maturation of the resulting SA progenitors in the presence of neurotrophic factors (BDNF, GDNF and NGF) resulted in the induction of a high yield of sympathetic neurons/progenitors co-expressing PHOX2B together with the sympathetic neuron regulator GATA3 (Tsarovina et al., 2010) (average of 40% of total cells), ASCL1 (63%) and the SA differentiation regulator ISL1 (64%) (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in the figures.

claims.claim: At later stages of differentiation almost all PHOX2B-GFP+ cells co-expressed ASCL1 further confirming a gradual transition from an early ASLC1+PHOX2B- progenitor to a more 'mature' double positive state.
claims.source: At later stages of differentiation almost all PHOX2B-GFP + cells co-expressed ASCL1 further confirming a gradual transition from an early ASLC1+PHOX2B- progenitor to a more 'mature' double positive state (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data not shown in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A high proportion of the resulting sympathetic neurons expressed the catecholamine production-associated enzyme/sympathetic neuron markers tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) together with dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH).
claims.source: A high proportion of the resulting cells also expressed the catecholamine production-associated enzyme/sympathetic neuron markers tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) (Figure 5D) together with dopamine- β-hydroxylase (DBH) (Ernsberger et al., 2000) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The sympathetic neuron cultures widely expressed the peripheral nervous system marker PERIPHERIN (PRPH) together with the trunk axial marker HOXC9.
claims.source: Furthermore, the cultures widely expressed the peripheral nervous system marker PERIPHERIN (PRPH) (Troy et al., 1990) together with the trunk axial marker HOXC9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Dramatic induction of GATA3, ASCL1, TH and PHOX2B transcripts (between 1000 and 1,000,000-fold) as well as other SA lineage markers such as GATA2, DBH and to a lesser extent PHOX2A was detected using qPCR.
claims.source: We also detected dramatic induction of GATA3, ASCL1, TH and PHOX2B transcripts (between 1000 and 1,000,000-fold) as well as other SA lineage markers such as GATA2, DBH and to a lesser extent PHOX2A using qPCR (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Following depolarising current injection, the sympathetic neurons were found to fire either a single action potential (AP) at the stimulus onset (type I) or a sequence of 'regenerative' APs (type II).
claims.source: Following depolarising current injection, the neurons were found to fire either a single action potential (AP) at the stimulus onset (type I) or a sequence of 'regenerative' APs (type II) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Similar electrophysiological responses have been previously reported to be indicative of in vitro derived sympathetic neurons.
claims.source: Similar electrophysiological responses have been previously reported to be indicative of in vitro derived sympathetic neurons (Oh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The outward potassium currents in the Type I cells activated at significantly more hyperpolarised potentials than those in the Type II cells, which would be the likely cause of the different spiking characteristics observed in these cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that the outward potassium currents in the Type I cells activated at significantly more hyperpolarised potentials than those in the Type II cells, which would be the likely cause of the different spiking characteristics observed in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The sympathetic neurons secrete the catecholamines dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE).
claims.source: We also confirmed that our sympathetic neurons secrete the catecholamines dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) further confirming their functionality (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The most efficient route toward the production of sympathoadrenal cells and functional sympathetic neurons from hPSCs relies on the induction of posterior axial progenitors.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that the most efficient route toward the production of sympathoadrenal cells and functional sympathetic neurons from hPSCs relies on the induction of posterior axial progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing efficient generation of sympathoadrenal cells from axial progenitor-derived trunk NC.

claims.claim: The in vitro generation of trunk NC cells from hPSCs remains challenging and requires FACS-sorting of selected progenitor subpopulations.
claims.source: Despite progress in the optimisation of current NC differentiation protocols the in vitro generation of trunk NC cells from hPSCs remains challenging and requires FACS-sorting of selected progenitor subpopulations, a time-consuming and laborious process associated with increased cell death.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claims.claim: Previous work in amniote embryos suggested that posterior (trunk/lumbosacral) NC cells arise independently from their anterior counterparts, within a pool of axial progenitors localised near the primitive streak and the tailbud during axis elongation.
claims.source: Previous work in amniote embryos suggested that posterior (trunk/lumbosacral) NC cells arise independently from their anterior counterparts, within a pool of axial progenitors localised near the primitive streak and the tailbud during axis elongation (Catala et al., 1995; Schoenwolf et al., 1985; Schoenwolf and Nichols, 1984; Wymeersch et al., 2016; Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The authors exploited their ability to induce T+ NM potent axial progenitors from hPSCs in order to use them as the optimal starting point for the efficient in vitro derivation of trunk NC (~50% HOXC9+SOX10+), SA progenitors (~70% PHOX2B-GFP+) and functional sympathetic neurons without the use of FACS sorting.
claims.source: Here we utilised these findings and exploited our ability to induce T+ NM potent axial progenitors from hPSCs in order to use them as the optimal starting point for the efficient in vitro derivation of trunk NC (~50% HOXC9+ SOX10+), SA progenitors (~70% PHOX2B-GFP+) and functional sympathetic neurons without the use of FACS sorting.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: This strategy represents a considerable improvement over current approaches, which typically yield 5–10% PHOX2B-GFP+ cells.
claims.source: This strategy represents a considerable improvement over current approaches, which typically yield 5–10% PHOX2B-GFP + cells (Oh et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous work supported by a citation.

claims.claim: This strategy is in line with a recent study reporting the successful production of chromaffin-like cells through the use of an NC-induction protocol which transiently produces T+SOX2+ cells.
claims.source: and is in line with a recent study reporting the successful production of chromaffin-like cells through the use of an NC-induction protocol which transiently produces T+ SOX2+ cells (Denham et al., 2015; Abu-Bonsrah et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Similar to neural cells a HOX-positive posterior identity is acquired by human NC cells via two distinct routes: posterior cranial/vagal/cardiac HOX PG(1-5)+ NC cells emerge through the RA/WNT-induced posteriorisation of a default anterior precursor, whereas HOX PG(5-9)+ trunk NC cells arise from a separate WNT/FGF-induced posterior axial progenitor exhibiting caudal lateral epiblast/NMP features mixed with a neural plate border/neural crest identity.
claims.source: We show that, similar to neural cells a HOX-positive posterior identity is acquired by human NC cells via two distinct routes: posterior cranial/vagal/cardiac HOX PG(1-5)+ NC cells emerge through the RA/WNT-induced posteriorisation of a default anterior precursor, reflecting Nieuwkoop's 'activation-transformation' model, whereas HOX PG(5-9)+ trunk NC cells arise from a separate WNT/FGF-induced posterior axial progenitor exhibiting caudal lateral epiblast/NMP features mixed with a neural plate border/neural crest identity (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study shown in the model figure.

claims.claim: This finding offers an explanation for the failure of current RA posteriorisation-based in vitro differentiation protocols to yield high numbers of HOX9+ trunk NC cells.
claims.source: This finding offers an explanation for the failure of current RA posteriorisation-based in vitro differentiation protocols (Huang et al., 2016; Fattahi et al., 2016) to yield high numbers of HOX9+ trunk NC cells
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: The findings should serve as the conceptual basis for the design of experiments aiming to generate NC cells of a defined A-P character from hPSCs.
claims.source: and should serve as the conceptual basis for the design of experiments aiming to generate NC cells of a defined A-P character from hPSCs.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claims.claim: A subpopulation of in vitro derived human axial progenitors acquires border/early NC characteristics in response to the WNT and FGF signals present in the differentiation culture media, and possibly under the influence of autocrine BMP signalling.
claims.source: Our data indicate that a subpopulation of in vitro derived human axial progenitors acquires border/early NC characteristics in response to the WNT and FGF signals present in the differentiation culture media, and possibly under the influence of autocrine BMP signalling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing co-expression of T and NC markers and the presence of BMP signalling.

claims.claim: Bulk and single cell transcriptome data show that mouse embryonic axial progenitors/NMPs express border and early NC markers.
claims.source: This is in line with bulk and single cell transcriptome data showing that mouse embryonic axial progenitors/NMPs express border and early NC markers (Gouti et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: An 'unstable', pre-neural plate border domain, potentially defined by the co-localisation of pre-neural (Nkx1-2) and border markers such as Pax3 and Msx1, arises in the avian embryonic caudal lateral epiblast in response to autocrine BMP, FGF and possibly WNT signalling.
claims.source: Furthermore, our data reflect findings in the chick embryo showing that an 'unstable', pre-neural plate border domain, potentially defined by the co-localisation of pre-neural (Nkx1-2) (Delfino-Machín et al., 2005) and border markers such as Pax3 (Bang et al., 1997) and Msx1, arises in the avian embryonic caudal lateral epibllast in response to autocrine BMP, FGF (Streit and Stern, 1999) and possibly WNT signalling (LaBonne and Bronner-Fraser, 1998).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: CDX2 expression is maintained at high levels during the generation of trunk NC indicating that this transcription factor might be critical in inducing an NC character in axial progenitors.
claims.source: We also found that CDX2 expression is maintained at high levels during the generation of trunk NC indicating that this transcription factor might be critical in inducing an NC character in axial progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of maintained CDX2 expression.

claims.claim: CDX2 has been shown, together with β-catenin, to bind and activate neural plate border/early NC specifiers such as MSX1 and ZIC1.
claims.source: CDX2 has been shown, together with β-catenin, to bind and activate neural plate border/early NC specifiers such as MSX1 and ZIC1 (Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2016; Funa et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: ChiP-Seq data from in vitro-derived mouse NMPs have revealed that many NC/border genes are direct targets of CDX2 often jointly with T (e.g. PAX3, SOX9, ZIC3).
claims.source: and, intriguingly, ChiP-Seq data from in vitro-derived mouse NMPs have revealed that many NC/border genes are direct targets of CDX2 often jointly with T (e.g. PAX3, SOX9, ZIC3) (Amin et al., 2016).
